Emotions

Why do I get angry over little things?

Sometimes the spark is small, but the fuel had been building up for hours: hunger, sleep loss, hurry or worries.

You drop a spoon and let out an outsized yell. Someone is slow to pull away at the lights and your blood boils. Later, calmer, the intensity of your reaction surprises you. It is not unusual: anger almost never depends solely on what triggers it.

Your body's state matters

Several studies show that tiredness and hunger make us more irritable. In a 2019 experiment, Zlatan Krizan and Garrett Hisler restricted a group's sleep for two nights: faced with irritating noises, they felt angrier than those who had slept well. That same year, Jennifer MacCormack and Kristen Lindquist showed that hunger increases the chance of interpreting an ambiguous situation as hostile, especially when we do not realise we are hungry.

The explanation is that the brain interprets bodily sensations according to context. If we feel tense and unwell, and something goes wrong at that moment, it is easy to pin all the discomfort on that little thing.

Venting does not always vent

It is often said that hitting a cushion or shouting helps release anger. In an experiment by Brad Bushman, angry people who hit a punchbag while thinking about the person who had offended them were later more aggressive than those who did nothing. A 2024 meta-analysis confirmed that activities that increase arousal, such as hitting, do not reduce anger, while those that lower it, such as slow breathing or relaxation, do.

Naming it and stepping back

Putting what we feel into words ("I'm frustrated because I expected something else") reduces the intensity of the emotion, something also seen in neuroimaging studies. Another useful strategy is distance: thinking about the situation as if it were happening to someone else, or asking how it will look in a week's time. Ethan Kross has shown that talking to yourself in the second or third person ("what's wrong, Anna?") helps you calm down.

What usually helps

  • Check the "tank". Before reacting, ask yourself whether you are hungry, tired, rushed or carrying a background worry.
  • Name the emotion. Telling yourself "I'm really irritated" helps you step back and not act at once.
  • Give it a few minutes. The physical arousal of anger falls if it is not fed with more thoughts of grievance. Going for a walk or breathing slowly helps more than "venting" by shouting or hitting something.
  • Come back to it later. If there was a real problem behind it, it is easier to discuss once the storm has passed.
If anger is frequent, makes you lose control, damage things or hurt other people, it is worth seeking professional help. There are effective treatments for managing it.
